opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it wasn't one moment so much as a shift in what kinds of failures we were seeing.

For years in robotics, every new task was its own project. You'd collect data for picking up a cup, train a policy, and it would work in that kitchen, under that lighting, with that cup. Move it to a different room or hand it a slightly different object, and performance would just fall off a cliff. Progress felt linear at best: more engineering, more task-specific data, a bit more capability.

What changed is that when we started training large models on diverse data across many tasks, and especially when we brought in vision-language models pretrained on internet-scale data, we started seeing generalization we never explicitly trained for. You could ask the robot to "move the banana to the picture of Taylor Swift," or pick up "the extinct animal" from a set of toys, and it would do it. Nobody had collected robot demonstrations for those concepts. The semantic knowledge was coming from the web, and the model was grounding it into actions. That was the moment where I thought, okay, this isn't just a better policy. This is a different way of building robots.

The second thing was scaling behavior. In classical robotics, adding more data didn't reliably help, and sometimes it hurt because of interference between tasks. With these models, we saw that more diverse data, more embodiments, and bigger models generally made things better, including on tasks the model hadn't seen. Positive transfer across robots and tasks is something the field had wanted for a long time, and it started to actually show up.

And third, the failures became more interesting. Instead of "the gripper missed by two centimeters because the object was slightly rotated," the failures started to look like reasoning failures or physical-understanding failures, things like misjudging how something would deform or slip. That tells you the bottleneck has moved. The model understands what you want; now the hard part is the physics, the dexterity, the reliability.

So to be clear, we're not at the point where you can drop a robot into any home and have it do your laundry. Reliability, safety, and dexterous manipulation are still very real challenges. But the trajectory changed. We went from hand-crafting each skill to having a foundation that generalizes, and once you have that, the question becomes how fast you can scale the data and close the loop, not whether it's possible at all. That felt like a step change to me.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was watching the models do things we never trained them to do.

For most of my time working on robot learning, the pattern was painfully consistent. You'd collect data for a task, train a policy, and it would work on that task, in that lab, with that lighting, with those objects. Move the table six inches, swap the mug for a different mug, and it would fall apart. Every new capability cost you a whole new data collection effort. That's not a path to general robots, that's a treadmill.

What changed for me was the moment we started building on top of large vision-language models and saw transfer that had no business being there. You'd ask the robot to pick up the extinct animal, and it would reach for the toy dinosaur, even though nothing in the robot data ever mentioned dinosaurs or extinction. The semantic knowledge from the internet-scale pretraining was flowing into the motor behavior. That's qualitatively different from a policy that's a little more robust. It means the robot has a world model it didn't get from the robot data, and it can use it.

The second thing was the scaling behavior. In the old regime, more data gave you diminishing returns pretty fast, because you were just memorizing one setup more thoroughly. Once we had a model that could absorb data across many robot embodiments, many labs, many tasks, we saw performance keep climbing as we added more. The curves looked like language model curves, not like classical robotics curves. When you see that, you start to believe the recipe generalizes, and the bottleneck shifts from "can we make it work" to "how much data can we get through the pipeline."

And the third piece is just how fast the gap closed on dexterity. Things like folding laundry or doing fine manipulation were considered years away, and then within a year or so of these foundation-model approaches, you had models doing them with reasonable reliability. Not perfect, but on a trajectory. When the hard problems stop being special cases and start being just another thing the general model gets better at with scale, that's when I stopped thinking of it as incremental progress and started thinking of it as a step change.

r002.rationale: The speaker says the models did things they were never trained to do and describes that unexpected transfer as what changed their view from incremental progress to a step change.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key question is whether a robot can use what it learned in one situation to handle a different one. Getting a robot to do a task reliably is valuable, but if every new object or instruction requires a whole new engineering effort, you’re still working within the old paradigm.

What would convince me of a real step change is transfer: you teach the model something, and that makes it better at other tasks you didn’t explicitly train it to do. Can it handle an unfamiliar object? Can it respond to a different way of asking for the same thing? Can it recover when the situation changes?

And I’d distinguish that from a compelling demo. You want repeated trials, unfamiliar environments, and a clear accounting of failures. The exciting possibility is that we’re building a shared foundation for many robot skills. The evidence has to be that adding experience makes that foundation more broadly useful.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key question is whether a robot can take what it learned in one situation and use it in another. Getting a robot to perform a task you’ve carefully trained it for is exciting, but it doesn’t necessarily change how you build the next capability.

The more significant shift is when training across different tasks starts to help with a new task—when you can change the instruction, the objects, or the environment, and the robot can still do something useful. Then you’re starting to get a reusable model rather than a separate system for every behavior.

I wouldn’t equate that with robotics being solved. Reliability is still a very high bar. But that ability to transfer is what would convince me that we’re on a different trajectory.
